newsitem.title: USA: Industry questions U.S. climate draft plan.
newsitem.headline: Industry questions U.S. climate draft plan.

text.p: U.S. industries raised concern Thursday that the Clinton administration was going to wait until the last minute in international talks to reveal its position on targets and deadlines for curbing greenhouse gas emissions, which might bar debate on the options.

The Global Climate Coalition, which represents big producers and consumers of fossil fuels, also questioned how compliance with a new international agreement would be monitored and how baselines for trading emissions credits would be set.

The concerns surrounded administration proposals released last week calling for legally binding limits on industrialized countries' emissions, and a scheme for countries which pollute below the cap to sell emissions credits to bigger polluters. Calling the proposal "ambitious and assertive," coalition executive director John Shlaes said he feared Washington was rushing into an agreement that could be binding for 50 years.

"We're going to have to have that discussion on impacts on the United States before we get to Kyoto," Shlaes said at a news conference, referring to talks on a new international climate agreement which will close in Japan in December.

Assistant Secretary of State Eileen Claussen said the administration would finish its analysis of the impact of various emissions cuts and timetables by the end of March, and the work would then be open to public comment.

"To suggest that we won't have some opportunities to share data and to look at the impacts is contrary to everything we've said since the beginning of this process and is made up to scare people," she said in a telephone interview.

The broad U.S. position on targets and timetables would be apparent by June, she said, when a draft agreement with ranges of options for targets and timetables would be circulated among all countries.
"There will have to be a range of levels and a range of dates in it," she said.
Come December, "if it's not a viable agreement we won't sign onto it," Claussen said, adding that the United States would not sign onto any targest or timetables which it could not meet itself.
She dismissed concerns by Shlaes that the United Nations would be involved in monitoring compliance with any agreement that is reached.

"There are parties to whatever convention. Those (review) teams would come from the parties," she said, pointing to a similar recent review of U.S. compliance with existing emissions reduction targets by a team from other countries.
